vignette:
Mika, at 63, carries the weight of stories, not just those he publishes, but the one etched into his own being. Before the disaster, he was a vibrant presence, a man whose passion for literature fueled a thriving publishing house. He loved the smell of ink and paper, the intellectual hum of a manuscript in progress, the thrill of discovering a new voice. His home, shared with his wife Leilani, often buzzed with friends and family, filled with laughter and the aroma of island cooking. He was known for his booming laugh and his ability to hold a room captive with an anecdote.

The turning point came five years ago, during the annual Pacific Literary Festival. Mika was at the launch of his company’s most anticipated novel, a grand affair held in a beautifully restored colonial-era building. He remembers the warmth of the crowd, the clinking of glasses, the author’s voice resonant over the microphone. Then, a low rumble, a sound that seemed to come from the very foundations of the earth. It wasn't an earthquake; it was something else, something man-made and catastrophic. The ceiling cracked, plaster rained down, and in a terrifying, deafening sequence, a section of the building imploded. Mika recalls a flash of blinding dust, the horrifying screams, the sensation of being thrown forward, crushed by falling debris. He remembers the acrid smell of pulverized concrete and the taste of blood in his mouth. He was trapped for what felt like an eternity, hearing the muffled cries of others, the desperate attempts at rescue. When he was finally pulled out, bruised and bleeding, he saw the devastation: mangled steel, shattered glass, and the haunting stillness of bodies covered by sheets. Two of his junior editors, bright young talents he had personally mentored, were among the casualties.

In the immediate aftermath, Mika’s physical injuries healed, but the invisible wounds began to fester. He tried to return to work, to the familiar rhythm of publishing, but everything felt off-kilter. The once-beloved office now felt like a cage. The sounds of the city outside – a sudden siren, the distant rumble of construction – would send a jolt of terror through him. He started having nightmares, vivid and relentless, reliving the collapse, the dust, the screams, the faces of his lost colleagues. He’d wake up in a cold sweat, Leilani gently stroking his arm, trying to soothe him back to sleep, but sleep offered no true escape.

Now, five years on, the echoes of that day still dominate his life. Mika still goes to the publishing house, but the joy has drained away. He finds himself constantly scanning the ceilings, subtly checking emergency exits, even in familiar spaces. A sudden loud noise – a dropped stack of books, a car backfiring outside – sends his heart racing, his muscles tensing. He’s become hyper-vigilant, always on edge, as if expecting another disaster to strike. His concentration, once sharp and focused, is shattered. Reading manuscripts, a task he once cherished, now feels like an insurmountable chore. He struggles to follow plotlines, his mind drifting, replaying fragments of the collapse, or fixating on the fragility of life. Deadlines, once a motivator, now induce a paralyzing anxiety. He delegates almost everything, finding excuses to avoid meetings, especially those in larger, older buildings.

At home, Leilani observes his quiet withdrawal. He rarely laughs anymore, his booming voice replaced by a low, almost inaudible murmur. He often sits staring out the window, his gaze distant, lost in a world she can’t reach. He feels a profound sense of guilt – why did he survive when others, younger, with so much more ahead of them, did not? This guilt gnaws at him, whispering that he doesn't deserve the peace he so desperately craves. He avoids any mention of the festival, the old building, or the colleagues he lost. The topic is too raw, too painful, stirring up a suffocating wave of shame and sorrow. He feels detached from his own life, from Leilani, from his friends. The world seems a dangerous, unpredictable place, and he, a mere survivor, is just waiting for the next catastrophe. He rarely finds pleasure in anything, the vibrant colors of his world dulled to a perpetual grey.
